network.prose: Peers of the Ergo proof-of-work network -- specifically, nodes whose MAIN chain contains block a7439dad316fc1f387871b9839660b3ad3ada657e6cb0a9a28d807b78346aba9 (mainnet height 1870000) and behind which at least 2749641828372274216960 units of cumulative work have been done. That is not a list of addresses and deliberately not one: an Ergo node's peers are whoever is on the chain at the time it starts, so what is declared here is the property they must have, and the node running this service is what turns that property into addresses. They arrive at launch in this instance's __config__, as the ConfigurationFile.NetworkResolution whose tags contain 'pow:ergo'; service/entrypoint.sh reads every peer_instances[].uri_slot[].uri out of it and writes them into scorex.network.knownPeers before starting the jar. Nothing here asks for open egress, and nothing here names a host: an empty resolution starts the node with knownPeers = [] rather than falling back to a list this file would have had to hardcode. The cumulative-work figure is the one the chain itself had reached AT that block, not at any later tip, so the ask says 'a peer that has at least caught up to the block I named' and stays exactly as strict tomorrow as it is today; pow.min_height restates the same fact in the form the resolver can check from /info alone, before it spends two more requests on the block itself. pow.max_tip_age_s is what keeps a pinned block from turning into a weaker and weaker ask as the chain moves on: a peer stalled an hour behind is no use for bootstrapping, whatever it once verified.

protocol_stack.prose: Ergo's own peer-to-peer protocol, which is what a knownPeers entry is dialled with -- not the REST API this service exposes on 9053. The distinction matters at the resolver's end: a peer is verified over REST and has to be reached over P2P, and those are two ports on the same host.
